analysis.one_liner: Lets unions require workers to pay union fees even in right-to-work states.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote; it died in the Senate committee to which it was referred.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current federal labor law, states can pass 'right-to-work' laws that bar union contracts from requiring workers to join or pay fees to the union that represents them — even though federal law requires the union to represent every worker in the workplace. This bill would repeal that state authority, so union agreements could require membership or fees nationwide. It was referred to the Senate labor committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Unions and unionized workers. Unions would stop having to represent non-paying workers in right-to-work states, which they say drains resources and weakens bargaining. Union members would get stronger collective bargaining. Workers who choose not to pay could be required to do so as a condition of their job.

how_it_helps.text: Federal law requires unions to bargain for every worker in a workplace, and Section 14(b) lets states exempt those workers from paying for the representation they receive; repealing it ends that imbalance. [S2] [S3]
The bill amends the National Labor Relations Act so labor agreements may require membership in a union regardless of state law. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Workers in the more than two dozen right-to-work states who would have to pay union dues or fees as a condition of employment, and employers who lose a state-law tool that weakens unions in their workplaces.

drawbacks.text: The bill would override the laws of right-to-work states, requiring workers who want no union relationship to pay dues or fees anyway to keep their jobs. [S2] [S3]
Supporters of right-to-work laws argue compulsory fees violate workers' freedom of association and that states should set their own labor rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For union members the bill restores a 'free rider' fix — everyone who benefits from bargaining pays for it — and stronger unions generally mean better wages and benefits for represented workers. The cost falls on workers who would prefer not to fund a union, who would face a fee-or-leave choice, and on states whose right-to-work policies would be voided.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on September 19, 2017, joined by six other Senate Democrats. [S1] [S3]
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day. [S1] [S5]
No further action was recorded; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of compulsory union fees — employers and right-to-work advocates — benefit from the bill's death, since union fee requirements stay barred in right-to-work states. Unions in those states continue covering the cost of representing non-paying workers.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown, Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, Sen. Tammy Baldwin, Sen. Jeff Merkley, Sen. Ed Markey, Sen. Maggie Hassan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill alongside Warren as original cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the Senate agenda and the HELP Committee in the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Controlled the committee and floor agenda under which the bill was never considered.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or allied Independents; no Republican supported the bill, and the Republican-run committee and Senate never considered it. [S4] [S5]

industries.note: The bill would let union contracts require membership or fee payment nationwide, ending the free-rider problem in right-to-work states where unions must represent non-paying workers. Stronger union finances generally support better bargaining outcomes for represented workers.
Employers would lose a state-law framework that keeps unions financially weaker; they would face workplaces where union fee agreements are enforceable under federal law.
